title: Tamsin and the Glasshouse
premise: Tamsin Coral Galloway has spent thirty years as the night librarian of a city that never fully sleeps, cataloguing silences the way others catalogue books. When renovation crews tear open her childhood home and a box of undelivered letters surfaces behind her mother's wardrobe, Tamsin learns that her family's careful architecture — her father's absence, her sister's marriage, her mother's cheerfulness — was arranged around a single unspoken truth: Tamsin was given away at birth and quietly taken back, and everyone chose to forget. As her mother's memory begins to fail, Tamsin must decide whether to deliver the letters and shatter the family's fragile peace, or preserve the lie that made her belong. She chooses truth, reading the letters aloud to her mother in the glasshouse, and in the wreckage discovers that belonging was never the reward for silence — it was what survived it.
about_author: Astrid Yarrow is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private correspondence donated to regional libraries, an experience that left her convinced every family is a locked room with one key. She writes from a converted glasshouse on the coast, where she keeps her own unsent letters in a box she swears she will one day post.

chapters.title: The Hours Nobody Claims
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Tamsin's POV. We meet Tamsin among the sleeping readers of the night library, a woman who has made invisibility an art form, cataloguing not books but the things her family never says. A call from her sister Ivy: the childhood house is being sold, and Mother must be moved. Tamsin agrees to help pack, dreading the return. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of a carefully managed distance.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Packing her mother's bedroom, Tamsin pries loose the wardrobe panel and finds a biscuit tin of letters, all addressed to her, all undelivered, spanning thirty years, in her mother's handwriting and — shockingly — her father's. She pockets three but cannot open them. Emotional beat: the floor of her ordered life tilting; curiosity at war with self-protection.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Unsaid
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, interwoven with a library patron's story she quietly helps. Tamsin reads the first letters and learns the shape of the secret: she was surrendered at birth, then reclaimed, and the family agreed never to speak of it. She begins keeping a literal inventory of the family's silences, her professional habit turned weapon. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with a terrible relief — the invisibility was designed.

chapters.title: Ivy, Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Ivy's POV. Ivy, the sister who never left, tends their mother Edith and resents Tamsin's safe remove. She notices Tamsin acting strangely and suspects the letters have surfaced; she has known for years and was made to promise. A tense kitchen scene where both sisters say everything except the thing. Emotional beat: loyalty as a shared burden that has curdled into resentment.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, fragmentary and luminous. In her failing memory, past and present blur; she tends the glasshouse plants and half-addresses Tamsin as someone else — 'the little one who came back.' Edith almost tells the truth, then loses the thread. Tamsin watches, aching to ask. Emotional beat: tenderness and frustration; the reader sees the mother's love was always tangled with guilt.

chapters.title: What the Father Wrote
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin tracks down her father, Malcolm, living alone two towns over, and confronts him with his own letters. He admits the arrangement was his condition for returning: no one would ever name what happened. He begs her to let it stay buried, revealing he is ill and wants peace, not reckoning. Emotional beat: the seductive logic of silence; Tamsin almost accepts it.

chapters.title: The Librarian's Error
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, crisis of self. Tamsin realizes her whole identity — the night shifts, the catalogued silences, the refusal of intimacy — was built to match the family's fiction. She nearly destroys the letters in the library incinerator, then cannot. Her estranged friend and colleague Nell confronts her: 'You've been returning yourself to sender for thirty years.' Emotional beat: the dark night of the self; choosing between the lie that protects and the truth that frees.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Ivy's POV. Edith is hospitalized after a fall; doctors confirm rapid cognitive decline. Ivy, terrified of losing her mother before reconciling, finally breaks her promise and tells Tamsin everything from her side — how she found out at nineteen and carried it alone. The sisters fight, then grieve together. Emotional beat: rupture becoming repair; loyalty redefined as truth-telling, not secret-keeping.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV — the climax. In the glasshouse, with Edith lucid in a rare clear hour, Tamsin reads the letters aloud, one by one: her mother's guilt, her father's fear, the day of the surrender, the day of the return. Edith listens, weeps, and answers the question the family arranged itself around: 'We thought we were protecting you. We were protecting ourselves.' Emotional beat: catharsis; the family myth dismantled in an afternoon of plain speech.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue in motion. Months later: Edith in the glasshouse of her new care home, Tamsin visiting in daylight for the first time, the letters boxed and labeled — not hidden, but archived, given to Edith to reread on her good days. Tamsin mails one final letter of her own, to her father, and takes a job cataloguing an archive of found correspondence. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — belonging rebuilt on truth, invisibility traded for presence.
